transcript.text: Alright everyone, let's get this greenlight meeting started. We've got a potential deal here — an international airline wants to license the independent concert documentary for their passenger-entertainment system. The buyer's draft proposes a worldwide, twelve-month, non-exclusive license using the current picture and delivery master. Before I can sign off on this, I need our rights, music, and post-production leads to report any approval conditions. Let's hear from each of you — are there any issues or conditions we need to address before I approve these terms and delivery instructions?
transcript.speaker: A1

transcript.text: I need to flag a significant rights issue. I reviewed the executed performer agreements yesterday, and they only permit licensing of the documentary in the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom — not worldwide as the buyer's draft proposes. Additionally, the agreements limit us to a six-month non-exclusive term, not twelve months. The agreements also require a written rights amendment before we can deliver. I should note that the buyer's draft arrived after I completed my review of these agreements.
transcript.speaker: A2

transcript.text: I have a music clearance issue to report. I checked the publisher's clearance ledger this morning and confirmed that the current cut's use of the song 'Afterglow Avenue' lacks the synchronization clearance required for airline distribution. The cleared replacement is 'Night Transit.' I haven't updated the music cue sheet yet because the final territory and term were still unsettled — but given that we're now looking at this deal, we'll need to swap in 'Night Transit' and update the cue sheet before any delivery master goes out.
transcript.speaker: A3

transcript.text: I need to flag a post-production delivery issue. I completed the airline's ingest test with the delivery vendor today, and the required master is 1080p SDR video with stereo Lt/Rt audio and English SDH captions as a sidecar VTT file. Our current 4K master uses a different audio and caption package, so it won't meet their spec. I have not issued the revised export order yet while licensing terms remain pending — we'll need to create a new delivery master to their specifications before anything goes out.

transcript.text: Thank you all for those critical findings. Let me summarize what I'm hearing: Jonah, the performer agreements restrict us to US, Canada, and UK only — not worldwide — and cap the non-exclusive term at six months, not twelve. We'd also need a written rights amendment before delivery. Leila, 'Afterglow Avenue' lacks sync clearance for airline distribution, so we need to swap in 'Night Transit' and update the cue sheet before any master goes out. Owen, the airline requires a 1080p SDR master with stereo Lt/Rt audio and English SDH captions as a sidecar VTT file — our current 4K master won't work, and Owen hasn't issued the revised export order yet. So clearly, the buyer's draft as written can't be approved as-is. Before I make a decision, I want to confirm with each of you: Jonah, can we realistically negotiate a written rights amendment with the performers to cover the airline territory and six-month term before delivery? And do you recommend we push back on the buyer to accept the restricted territory (US, Canada, UK) and six-month term rather than their proposed worldwide twelve-month terms? Leila, are there any costs or timing concerns with the 'Night Transit' swap and cue sheet update? Owen, what's the turnaround time on creating the new 1080p SDR delivery master with the revised audio and caption package? I need to know if these conditions are all feasible within a reasonable timeframe so I can decide whether to approve with conditions or send this back to the buyer for renegotiation.
transcript.speaker: A1

transcript.text: Thanks, Mara. On your first question — whether we can realistically negotiate a written rights amendment with the performers — I want to be straightforward: I've confirmed what the executed agreements allow, but I have not yet had any conversations with the performers or their representatives about amending those terms. So I can't give you a reliable estimate on timeline or likelihood of getting an amendment approved without first reaching out to them. I'd recommend we don't commit to the buyer on any expanded terms until we've at least gauged the performers' willingness. On your second question — whether I recommend pushing back on the buyer to accept the restricted territory and six-month term — yes, absolutely. Our current rights are limited to US, Canada, and UK for six months non-exclusive. We cannot lawfully deliver a worldwide, twelve-month license. I recommend we go back to the buyer with our actual available rights and see if they'll accept a US/Canada/UK, six-month non-exclusive deal. If they insist on broader territory or a longer term, that's contingent on us successfully negotiating amendments with the performers, and we should not promise what we haven't secured. I'd also flag that the written amendment needs to be executed before delivery — not after — so the sequencing matters.

The main work items are: updating the music cue sheet to reflect the substitution, and then coordinating with Owen's team to ensure the new delivery master incorporates the replacement track rather than 'Afterglow Avenue.' In terms of timing, the cue sheet update itself is straightforward — I can have it completed quickly once we have confirmed final territory and term, since those details feed into the cue sheet. I'd recommend we don't deliver any master until both the cue sheet is updated and the new export with 'Night Transit' is completed and verified. We need a fresh build from the ground up for this delivery.
